blocks.text: Data can also be text

std::string is a type from the standard library for storing a sequence of characters. To use it, add #include <string>; we still include <iostream> because we also produce output. These headers provide different facilities. The prefix std:: indicates that the name belongs to the standard library.

In std::string zona = "North";, zona is a variable, and "North" is the literal that supplies its initial value. The quotation marks delimit the literal in the code; they are not part of the characters stored or printed.

blocks.question: Fill in only the standard-library type needed to store the label Door A.
blocks.explanation: std::string represents a sequence of characters; <string> makes this type available.

blocks.text: Empty text is a valid state

std::string etiqueta; initializes a string to empty: it contains no characters. This guarantee differs from int cantidad; when cantidad is an uninitialized local integer variable. You can also write std::string etiqueta = ""; to make it clear that the string starts empty. Empty does not mean the variable does not exist.

blocks.question: What does std::string mensaje = ""; mean?
options: A text variable exists and its value contains zero characters.
The name mensaje has not been defined.
Reading the variable must produce a random number.
blocks.explanation: The object exists and its value is the empty string, which is valid for std::string.

blocks.text: Initial values depend on the type. Do not assume that an uninitialized local int starts empty just because a std::string does.
Assigning and copying text

A string can receive new text through assignment: zona = "South";. Another string can also be initialized from its value. As with the integers we studied earlier, the copy is independent. A later statement must explicitly update the copy if we want it to contain the new text.

blocks.explanation: registro received a copy of North; changing zona does not change registro.

blocks.question: Write only a string literal that assigns the word Closed to the variable estado.
blocks.explanation: Double quotation marks form a string literal; assignment replaces the previous value.

blocks.question: What changes when "South" is assigned to a std::string variable?
options: The identifier is automatically renamed South.
The type is converted into a number.
blocks.explanation: The object keeps its type and name; the stored sequence of characters changes.

blocks.text: Concatenation does not add quantities

Concatenating means building a string by placing one sequence after another. With std::string variables, + performs this operation: primera + segunda combines their characters in order. It does not insert spaces automatically. If we want a space, we must explicitly include it in the text. Concatenation creates a result; it does not change the variables that are only read.

The preceding literals are "Sector" and "West". The expression inserts the separator exactly once. Notice that "2" is text while 2 is an integer: similar-looking symbols can represent data with different roles.

blocks.text: Appending text to the existing state

cartel += " open"; appends a suffix and stores the result in cartel. For strings, += means adding characters to the current text, not adding a numeric quantity. We must include the leading space in the suffix to separate the words. Do not assume + behaves the same for every pair of quoted literals as it does for std::string: our calculations involve at least one std::string object.

blocks.explanation: anterior retains the original text; += changes cartel by appending the suffix.

The visible separation between Workshop and open.
The space between statements in the source file.
blocks.explanation: Concatenation does not insert spaces that are absent from its operands.

blocks.text: Build a label from data

In the lab, create two text variables: edificio = "Classroom" and codigo = "04". Build a third one, etiqueta, combining their values with a hyphen: Classroom-04. Print the label. On a second run, change only the initial literal of codigo to "07" and check that only this part of the output changes. Next, restore the initial literal "04" and, as a separate experiment, assign "07" to codigo after constructing etiqueta but before printing it: predict whether the already-built label updates automatically.
The second experiment revisits an idea about state: a stored result is a value obtained at a particular moment, not a formula that reruns automatically whenever its operands change.
Solution and a cumulative prediction
Changing the code before constructing the label changes the result. Changing it afterward leaves etiqueta unchanged; a new assignment must rebuild the text if we want to update it.

blocks.explanation: etiqueta received Area1 before the change. codigo now holds 2, but etiqueta is not recalculated.

blocks.text: Reference solution: Build and preserve a label
Consult this comparison after building and checking your own attempt. The reference shows one possible implementation; the criteria help identify other correct solutions.

Correctness criteria. edificio and codigo are text; etiqueta combines them with a hyphen and produces Classroom-04. If codigo is initially defined as "07", the result is Classroom-07. If codigo changes to "07" after etiqueta is built, the stored label keeps Classroom-04 until another concatenation is assigned to it. Preserve the leading zero and the distinction between text and numbers.

First test the reference version, then change only the initial literal of codigo to "07". For the state experiment, restore "04" and insert codigo = "07"; after defining etiqueta but before printing it: the output remains Classroom-04. To update it, you must run etiqueta = edificio + "-" + codigo; again after the change.
